**SHADOW STORIES — EPISODE 1: "MY MOUTH WASN'T MADE FOR ENGLISH"**
**Runtime:** 12-15 minutes
**Language:** A2/B1 accessible, flowing
**Format:** You on camera, text highlights on key sentences

---

I used to believe my mouth wasn't made for English.

I thought there was something broken inside me — something that other people had, but I didn't. Something in their brains, in their tongues, in the way their mouths moved that I would never have.

For years, I stayed silent. I smiled. I nodded. I pretended to understand when people spoke to me. But I never spoke back. Not really. Not in a way that mattered.

This is the story of how I found my voice. And if you've ever felt the same way — if you've ever sat in a room full of people speaking English and felt like you were invisible — this story is for you.

Let me start with a memory that still makes my chest tight.

I was four years old, sitting in a classroom in Florida. The teacher asked a simple question: "What did you eat for breakfast?"

I raised my hand. I was proud. I knew the answer.

"Cereal con leche," I said.

The teacher's face changed. Her smile disappeared. She looked angry. "Say it again."

I repeated the words. "Cereal con leche."

She asked again. And again. Her voice got louder each time. "In English. Say it in English."

I didn't understand what she wanted. I was saying the right answer — cereal with milk. But I was saying it in Spanish, because that's the only language I knew.

The other children were staring. I could feel their eyes on me. I could hear someone giggling. My face got hot. My eyes filled with tears.

I started to cry.

That day, something broke inside me. I made a decision that would shape the next fifteen years of my life.

I would never speak in class again.

I kept that promise. For fifteen years, I stayed silent. I wrote answers on paper. I nodded. I smiled. But I never spoke.

Years later, I heard about another child who made the same decision. A little girl named Fiorella. Same age. Same situation. Same shame.

When I heard her story, my chest got tight again. Because I knew exactly how she felt. That same moment of confusion. That same hot face. Those same tears.

That same decision to disappear.

But Fiorella's story doesn't end there. And neither does mine.

Let me tell you about another child. A boy I'll call Tieming.

He was six years old when his family moved from China to Singapore. On his first day of school, he walked into a classroom where everyone was speaking a language he didn't understand.

The teacher spoke. He didn't know what she said.

The students laughed. He didn't know why.

He sat at his desk feeling invisible. He didn't even know the English word for "homework." He didn't know the word for "desk." He didn't know the word for "confused."

One day, his teacher asked him about a spelling test. Tieming didn't understand what a spelling test was. He didn't study. He didn't know he was supposed to.

When the test started, he sat there with a blank paper. He wrote nothing.

His teacher walked over to his desk. Her face was red with anger. I can still picture it — that red face, those angry eyes, the way she moved.

She grabbed his backpack. She walked to the window. And she threw it outside — four floors down, into a pond.

Tieming was seven years old.

He sat there in shock while his classmates watched. Nobody said a word. Nobody helped him. Nobody stood up for him.

That night, he went home and cried for hours.

But here's what happened next.

His mother made a decision. Every morning, Tieming would wake up at 4:30 AM. He would sit at the kitchen table and read books in Chinese and English. He would check the dictionary again and again until his eyes hurt.

He hated it. Some mornings, he begged his mother to let him sleep. But she wouldn't.

His classmates called him a slow learner. His teachers said he would never succeed.

Nineteen years later, Tieming graduated from Newcastle University in England — with first-class honors.

He proved every single one of them wrong.

When I heard Tieming's story, I thought about my own mornings. The ones where I woke up early to practice English. The ones where I felt like giving up. The ones where I thought I would never get it right.

Tieming's story gave me hope. But it also made me angry. Angry that a teacher could do that to a child. Angry that nobody stopped her. Angry that so many of us have stories like this.

There was another boy. His name was Anderson, and he moved from Haiti to Connecticut.

He spoke only French Creole. Not a single word of English.

On his first day of school, he needed to use the bathroom. But he didn't know how to ask. He didn't know the words. So he just started walking.

He found two doors in the hallway. There were signs above them, but he couldn't read English. He picked one and walked inside.

He sat down. A few seconds later, the door burst open.

Someone started shouting at him. Asking questions. Fast. Loud. In English.

Anderson didn't understand anything. He just sat there, frozen. His heart was pounding. His hands were shaking.

When he finally walked out, there was a crowd of students in the hallway. They were all laughing. Pointing. Making sounds he didn't understand.

He had walked into the girls' bathroom.

He didn't know.

Anderson said that was the saddest day of his life. He wanted to disappear. He wanted to go back to Haiti where people understood him.

But he didn't give up.

He found a teacher who believed in him. He went to the library every single day after school. He practiced reading out loud, even when the words felt like rocks in his mouth.

Slowly, something changed. People started to understand him. And one day, he realized — he could understand them too.

When I heard Anderson's story, I remembered my own moments of confusion. The times I walked into the wrong room. The times I said the wrong thing. The times I wanted to disappear.

Anderson's story reminded me that I wasn't alone. That other people had felt this way. That other people had survived.

The last story I want to tell you is about a woman named Mirian.

She was a grandmother from Venezuela. She moved to America to be closer to her family, but she didn't speak any English.

She got a job at a nursing home, working in the laundry room. Simple work. Fold the sheets. Wash the towels. No talking required.

But nothing was simple.

Her manager would call her on the intercom. Mirian would hear her name, but she couldn't understand what came after it. She didn't respond. Her manager thought she was ignoring her.

When patients came to ask for extra blankets, Mirian had to guess what they wanted. Sometimes she guessed right. Sometimes she didn't.

She felt invisible. Like she existed in the world, but nobody could see her. Like she was a ghost, walking through rooms full of people who didn't know she was there.

But Mirian refused to stay invisible.

She asked her granddaughters to translate cartoons for her. She watched the news and tried to understand one word at a time. She found a program that helped her learn.

Word by word. Sentence by sentence. She built her voice from nothing.

And one day, she answered the intercom.

When I heard Mirian's story, I thought about my own grandmother. About the way she struggled with English. About the way she sometimes looked lost in conversations.

Mirian's story reminded me that it's never too late. That you can find your voice at any age. That you can build something from nothing.

Why am I telling you these stories?

Because I lived them too.

I grew up in the Democratic Republic of Congo. My first language is Lingala — a slow, soft language with sounds that feel like music.

When I tried to speak English, everything felt wrong. The sounds were too fast. The words got stuck in my throat. My tongue felt heavy and clumsy.

I would say something, and people would look confused. I would repeat it, and they still didn't understand.

I started to believe something was broken inside me. That my mouth wasn't built for this language. That some people could learn English, and I just... wasn't one of them.

So I stopped trying. I stayed quiet. I smiled and nodded my way through conversations, hoping nobody would ask me a direct question.

For years, I lived like that. Present, but silent. There, but invisible.

Then one day, I discovered something that changed everything.

I learned that the problem wasn't my mouth. It wasn't my brain. It wasn't my tongue.

The problem was the way I was trying to learn.

Here's what nobody told me about learning English.

You don't learn a language by memorizing rules. You learn it by hearing it — again and again — in a way you can understand.

Scientists call this "comprehensible input." It means listening to English that's just slightly above your level. Not too easy. Not too hard. Just right.

And there's something else. Something powerful.

It's called shadowing. You listen to a sentence, and you repeat it out loud. Not in your head — out loud. You copy the rhythm. The sounds. The feeling.

When you shadow, something magical happens. Your mouth learns to make the sounds. Your brain stops translating. You start to think in English.

This is how Tieming learned. Reading out loud every morning at 4:30 AM.

This is how Anderson learned. Practicing in the library until the words stopped feeling like rocks.

This is how Mirian learned. Repeating cartoons with her granddaughters.

This is how I learned.

Remember Fiorella? The little girl who said "cereal con leche" and decided to never speak again?

She grew up. She went to college. And she got a job that required her to stand in front of forty state senators — and read laws out loud, in English.

The girl who was too afraid to speak became a professional speaker.

When I heard that, I cried. Because I knew how hard that must have been. How many mornings she must have woken up scared. How many times she must have wanted to give up.

But she didn't. And neither did Tieming. And neither did Anderson. And neither did Mirian.

And neither did I.

Your mouth is not broken. Your brain is not slow. Your tongue is not the problem.

You just haven't found the right way to learn yet.

On this channel, I'm going to read stories with you. Simple stories. Powerful stories. Stories that will make you feel something.

And after each story, we'll practice together. You'll repeat after me. You'll shadow my voice. And slowly, sentence by sentence, you'll find your voice too.

If you felt something during this video — if you saw yourself in these stories — then subscribe.

Because Episode 2 is coming soon.

And I'll be reading it with you.

Sometimes I still hear that voice in my head. The one that says I'm not good enough. That my mouth wasn't made for this.

But then I remember Tieming at 4:30 in the morning. Anderson walking out of that bathroom. Mirian answering the intercom for the first time. Fiorella standing in front of those senators.

And I remember — they found their voice.

So can you.

---

**END**
